1.6 — Animation States: IsWalking, WalkDir, Attack

Your character moves through space, but it does not look alive yet — it plays the same idle animation no matter which way you walk. Today you connect your code to Unity's Animator state machine: reading its parameters, driving directional clips, flipping the sprite, and understanding why your code sets state while the engine plays frames.

Read the Docs ~15 min

In professional game engines, scripts rarely swap individual sprite images directly. Instead the visual engine uses an Animator Controller — a visual finite state machine. Your C# script communicates with it by setting parameters, and the controller decides which clip to play:

Unity APISignatureBehaviour
animator.SetBool() void SetBool(string name, bool value) Sets a boolean parameter. For persistent, continuous states such as idle versus walking.
animator.SetInteger() void SetInteger(string name, int value) Sets an integer parameter. For discrete multi-state selection such as a direction (0, 1, 2).
animator.SetTrigger() void SetTrigger(string name) Fires a momentary trigger that resets itself once a transition consumes it. For one-shot actions such as attacks or jumps.
spriteRenderer.flipX bool (read/write) Mirrors the sprite horizontally. Lets one sideways walk animation serve both left and right.
Mathf.Abs() float Mathf.Abs(float f) Returns a number's absolute value, stripping the sign. For comparing magnitudes regardless of direction.
GetComponentInChildren<T>() T GetComponentInChildren<T>() Finds a component on this GameObject or any of its children. You need this one — remember where the Sprite Renderer and Animator turned out to live.

Socratic: Separation of Concerns

  1. Why does your script set abstract parameters like "IsWalking" instead of telling the engine "play frame 4 of the walk sprite sheet"?
  2. If an artist replaced a 4-frame walk animation with an 8-frame one, how much C# would have to change? What does your answer say about the value of this split?
  3. What is the technical difference between setting a boolean with SetBool and firing an action with SetTrigger? Which one resets itself, and why does that matter for an attack?
  4. The Animator and the Sprite Renderer are on the child object, but your script is on the parent. Why does GetComponent<Animator>() return nothing, and what does GetComponentInChildren<Animator>() do differently?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Notice how each function and parameter type behaves in isolation, across completely different characters:

Example 1 — Setting a boolean state on a scuba diver:

// Drives a continuous state change (idle on the boat vs swimming underwater)
animator.SetBool("IsSwimming", waterDepth > 0f);

Example 2 — Selecting a discrete state on a warrior:

// Chooses an equipment stance: 0 = unarmed, 1 = sword and shield, 2 = greatsword
animator.SetInteger("WeaponStance", 2);

Example 3 — Firing a one-shot action on a wizard:

// Fires a momentary clip that plays once and returns to the default state
if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
{
    animator.SetTrigger("CastSpell");
}

Example 4 — Flipping a sprite on a flying falcon:

// Mirrors the sprite based on whether horizontal velocity is negative
spriteRenderer.flipX = horizontalVelocity < 0f;

Example 5 — Stripping signs with absolute value:

// Mathf.Abs turns -4.5 into +4.5, making magnitudes comparable regardless of direction
if (Mathf.Abs(steerX) >= Mathf.Abs(steerY))
{
    // horizontal magnitude is at least as strong as vertical
}

Predict Before Building

  1. If steerX is -0.8 and steerY is 0.3, what does Mathf.Abs(steerX) >= Mathf.Abs(steerY) evaluate to — and what would the player see as a result?
  2. In Example 1, waterDepth > 0f is itself a boolean expression. What value gets passed to SetBool when waterDepth is exactly 0?
  3. Example 4 compares velocity to zero. If the falcon is flying straight up, what is horizontalVelocity, and what happens to flipX? Is that what you want?
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Step 1 — read the Animator Controller in Unity. In the Overworld scene, select the child Sprite object under Player — remember from 1.2 that is where the Animator lives, not on the Player root. Then open Window → Animation → Animator.

  1. Click the Parameters tab in the top-left of the Animator window. Three parameters are already configured: IsWalking (Bool), WalkDir (Int), and Attack (Trigger). Someone built this state machine for you — your job is to drive it.
  2. Click the arrow from Walk_Horiz to Idle_Horiz. In the Inspector, read its condition: IsWalking is false.
  3. Click the arrows between the up, side, and down states. Notice they compare WalkDir to 0, 1, and 2. Write down which number means which direction — you will need these exact values in your code.
  4. Now click the arrow into any of the Shovel_Swing states. What two conditions must both be true before the attack animation plays?
Architectural specification for the animation half of PlayerController.cs:

Component references:

  • Which two components drive what you see — the picture itself, and the animation playback?
  • Both live on a child object. Which method finds components in children rather than on the root?
  • Which lifecycle method should cache those references so you look them up once instead of sixty times a second? What happens if you look them up in Update() instead?

A dedicated animation method:

  • Should animation logic be tangled into your movement calculation, or organised into its own helper method? Argue for your choice.
  • Where must that helper be called, so the visuals stay in sync with the input every frame?

Sub-problem 1 — evaluate the walking state:

  • How do you decide the character is moving in any direction? What condition checks whether either input is non-zero?
  • Which Animator method updates a boolean parameter, and what is the exact, correctly-capitalised name of the boolean in this controller?

Sub-problem 2 — evaluate direction and flip:

  • When moving diagonally, how do you decide whether the sideways or the vertical animation should play? How does Mathf.Abs() settle that argument?
  • If horizontal movement dominates: which integer means "sideways"? How do you decide whether flipX should be true or false from the direction of travel?
  • If vertical movement dominates: which integer means up, and which means down? Do you need to touch flipX at all when moving vertically — and if not, why not?

Sub-problem 3 — the attack trigger:

  • Which input function detects that the left mouse button (button index 0) was pressed this frame? Why is that different from asking whether it is currently held?
  • Which Animator method fires a one-shot trigger, and what is the trigger parameter called?

Save PlayerController.cs and return to Unity. Press Play and walk in all four directions. Your character should now blend between idle, walking sideways, walking up, and walking down, with the sprite flipping as it changes direction. Click to swing.

Bug Hunt: Diagnosing Animation Faults

  1. Misspell "IsWalking" as "isWalking" (lowercase i). What does the Unity Console report? Why is a misspelled parameter a loud error rather than a silent failure, and why is that a kindness?
  2. Which way is your character facing before you press any key at all? Select the Sprite object and look at Flip X on its Sprite Renderer. Does your idle animation point the way you expected?
  3. Comment out the line that sets flipX. Which direction can your character never face while walking sideways?
  4. Set WalkDir to a value the controller never checks — say 7. What happens to the animation, and what does that teach you about a state machine with no matching transition?
  5. Click the mouse rapidly. Does the attack animation trigger cleanly, and does it return to walking or idling afterwards?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Exploring state transitions

  1. Keep the Animator window open while the game runs in Play mode. Walk around. Watch the blue progress bar slide across each state and the transition arrows light up in real time. Which state is active when you stand still?
  2. Your Player is wired to Player_Shovel.controller — that is why the attack is a shovel swing. Now go find Assets/Artwork/Animations/Top_Down/PlayerAnimator/Axe/Player_Axe.controller and open it. It is a complete, working controller with axe swings instead of shovel swings, and it is not assigned to anything. What single property on the Animator component would you change to make your character swing an axe? (You will do exactly this in Unit 5.)
  3. Add a fourth parameter of your own to the controller and wire a transition to it. What is the minimum you need — a parameter, a state, and what else?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Open the Animator window and inspect states, arrows, and parameter conditions
  • Explain the distinct purposes of SetBool, SetInteger, and SetTrigger
  • Explain the architecture split: your code sets state parameters, the Animator Controller plays the clips
  • Say which WalkDir integer means up, sideways, and down
  • Use Mathf.Abs() to resolve which directional input dominates
  • Find a component on a child object with GetComponentInChildren
  • Commit your working animation integration to GitHub
